tests.description: A lone head, tail, grep, or cat of a saved-output path reads the store with no question and writes no copy. A folder from another machine still reads the store by name, and a name not in the store says it is no longer available. Reading a whole saved output back keeps one copy in the store. A chain that also reads a file on disk asks about that file only.

A line that only reads saved output runs in bash with no question, after a copy is written, and prints what the same line prints on a real file with the same text. A copy changed on disk is rewritten from the store before the next line.

sed has no rule, so a read of saved output with it asks std::exec and nothing more, and prints the right lines. A line that only names a saved output still asks std::bash, because no read of saved output was dropped.
A line safeBash cannot parse gets its copy before bash runs, found by a scan of the text, and a background job gets its copy before it starts.
A real program given a saved-output path from another machine's folder fails before any shell starts, with a message that names the path on this machine.

In `ln -sf <file> <saved output>; cat <saved output>`, the line does more than read, so the cat keeps its std::read question. With std::read rejected the line fails, so an approved link cannot turn into an unasked read.
A saved-output folder that other users can use, and a link planted where the folder goes, each fail the line before the shell starts.

A path that continues past a saved-output name is not a saved output. A look-alike folder reads the store in process and fails before a real program runs. A redirect into the folder, a delete of a saved output, and a listing of the folder are refused.
The stdlib's read takes a saved-output path as the whole filename, or the folder as dir, with offset and limit, and asks nothing. A folder from another machine reads the store by name.
